heading: 1 Introduction (1.1 Problem Background, 1.2 Restatement of the Problem)
note: Four background paragraphs, one per source, none quantified. 21 dates the concept to Essam El-Hinnawi in the 1970s and calls environmental displacement 'the negative feedback of man's transformation of nature' - the only framing sentence in the paper and it is rhetorical rather than analytical. 22 lists three degradation types (sea-level rise forcing Tuvalu to relocate, water shortage and drought, desertification driving Mexico-United States migration), each with a citation and no figure. 23 argues the 1951 Refugee Convention still has no clear conclusion on this group and cites the Kiribati case only by reference [3] here (the named case, Ioane Teitiota, appears later in 53, not here). 24 is the one paragraph that raises the real policy question - states' right to reject EDPs when they threaten national security, against the humanitarian argument - and leaves both positions standing. 25 turns normative ('the international community should actively seek multiple avenues of protection') and glues the '1.2 Restatement of the Problem' heading into its tail, so the paper's own problem statement is one sentence of exhortation. 26 states the client (ICM-F) and the three-part structure (planning, policy, application) and points at Figure 1, whose text is block 27. The chapter's whole contribution is the three-part division; no number, no definition and no task decomposition appears before the models start.

heading: 2 Assumptions (and 3 Glossary and Symbols, absorbed into block 50)
note: Six assumptions, and the measurement split every one of them into one printed line per block, so each group below is one paragraph of two to six measured blocks. Assumption 1 (29-34) says nationals prefer internal relocation because it is easier and because these countries are LDCs whose nationals mostly fail other countries' immigration standards - this is the assumption that carries the whole EDP count, since it makes the default outcome EIDPs rather than refugees, and it is the only one with figure support (Figure 2, block 35, 'Comparison of Some Countries'). Assumption 2 (36-37) treats sea-level rise as irreversible and excludes global cooling. Assumption 3 (38-40) freezes per-capita emissions and other pollutants before and after migration, which is what makes the environmental-impact formulas in 5.4 computable and is also the assumption most easily falsified by the evidence on migrant consumption. Assumption 4 (41-43) allows only ONE country in PEWS or EWS at a time, acknowledged by the international community - a scarcity rule with no basis and a decisive one, because it turns EDP numbers into a single-nation exercise. Assumption 5 (44-47) makes switching between legal and illegal activity costless, which is the premise of the crime model in 5.2. Assumption 6 (48-50) makes rational self-interest the only motive. Block 50's tail holds the entire '3 Glossary and Symbols' section - EWS, PEWS, KP, PA, CA, HS, CS, HB, OL, WL, CVS, GNH, SSI, GDP - inside one measured block, so chapter 3 has no blocks of its own and the glossary has no page of its own in the measurement. Note that CS means both 'Cultural Space' here and 'capital stock' in 4.3's notation, and that CS also appears as a country-industry share in the appendix.

heading: 4 Models for Planning (4.1 Number of People at Risk)
note: The counting rule, built by analogy to UNHCR's classification rather than by measurement. 51-52 are the chapter and section headings. 53 cites the issue paper and reference [4] to say the ambiguity of 'environmental refugees' is what trapped Ioane Teitiota of Kiribati, and 54 brings in UNHCR's three categories (refugees, asylum-seekers, IDPs) with Figure 3's caption inside the same block. Then two coined states: EWS, where national security is threatened by sea-level rise, extreme weather or drought AND the whole nation is predicted to be permanently uninhabitable in the near future (55-58); and PEWS, where the nation is predicted to enter EWS from historical data, suffers one of the three issues, and a large share of people is or will be affected (59-62). The third bullet (63-66) splits a declared-and-acknowledged PEWS population into Environmental Refugees, Environmental Asylum Seekers and EIDPs, all receiving equivalent UN rights. 67 derives the consequence from Assumption 1 - most nationals stay as EIDPs - and 68 states the EWS case, where the whole population becomes Environmental Refugees and the international community takes on relocation and culture protection. 69 is Figure 4's caption. 70 interprets with the one worked case: Tuvalu's 2001 declaration of failure makes it EWS, so its people are EDPs and Environmental Refugees, and 70's tail glues the '4.2 Cultural Value Evaluation System' heading. The defect is definitional circularity: EWS requires the nation to be 'predicted as permanently uninhabitable', the paper never states who predicts it or on what threshold, and the state is then used to classify the entire population as EDPs. Nothing in the chapter estimates a number, so the 'number of people at risk' promised by the heading is delivered as a labelling scheme - the only quantity in the paper's planning part is the Maldives figure used in chapter 6, and its derivation is never shown.

heading: 4.2 Cultural Value Evaluation System (4.2.1 Selection of Indicators, 4.2.2 Establishment of Evaluation System)
note: The culture index, adapted from the IUCN Red List and from a Chinese cultural-heritage evaluation literature. 71 routes it (culture as an unevaluated resource). 72 begins the indicator-selection argument and is cut mid-sentence by Figure 5's caption (73, 'Stratified Evaluation Index'); 74 completes it, taking Anderson's [7] index-selection principle and turning it into four principles - reference, feasibility, comprehensiveness, dominant - with no statement of how the four are applied. 75 is the lead-in to the eight indicator definitions, each of which the measurement split one line per block: historical buildings (76-78), oral language (79-82), written language (83), performing arts (84-85), custom activities (86-88), knowledge and practice (89-90), handicraft skills (91-92), cultural space (93-94). The definitions are qualitative and one of them states a testable relation - oral language uniqueness is 'inversely related to geographical area and population' - which is never used. 95 explains quantification (dimensionless treatment, Delphi plus paired comparison for weights, 'correcting each other') and 96 gives the actual scoring rule for the oral-language indicator: uniqueness as yes/no scoring 4 or 0, range (area) and population each banded into four levels (below 10, 10-50, 50-100, above 100 for area; up to 1,000, 1,000-5,000, 5,000-10,000, above 10,000 for users) scored 1-4, then rescaled to 100. The area bands are internally impossible (the cut-off 'more than 10' repeats a band the text already used for 'less than 10' - the top band is missing a unit) and the population bands are the ones actually applied. 97 describes the resulting system and 98 is Figure 7's caption; 99-113 then map the score ranges to IUCN-style categories. Two arithmetic defects: Near Threatened and Near Common are both given as 'between 40 and 60', so the two categories cannot be told apart, and Least Concern is 0-20 while the next band starts at 40, leaving 20-40 undefined; 'Extinct' is also misspelled 'Extincnt', and the Extinct definition keeps the Red List's species wording ('a taxon has disappeared'), which shows the adaptation was textual. 114 closes by calling the system developmental and glues the '4.3 EDPs Relocation Model' heading. The weights implied later (CSI = 0.28 HB + 0.39 WL + 0.32 OL in block 145) are said to be the cultural-value weights renormalised over three indicators, but 0.28 + 0.39 + 0.32 = 0.99, not 1, so the renormalisation does not close.

heading: 4.3 EDPs Relocation Model (destination country suitability index S, five indicators, AHP weights, two-objective planning)
note: The destination index S, five indicators, every one of them built in a handful of sentences. 115 routes it and splits the problem by state: for EWS nations relocation is an emergency so distance dominates; for PEWS nations demand, culture and destination features dominate. 116 names the five indicators - GNH, SSI, GDP, CPI, EPI - with SSI, CPI and EPI coined here and GNH and GDP imported. Each indicator follows the same pattern: prose split one printed line per block while it is introduced, then the formula. GNH (117-122) takes Bhutan's 1970 concept and writes GNH = II x UR x IF / Gini, i.e. income growth TIMES the unemployment rate TIMES inflation divided by the Gini coefficient; as printed, higher unemployment and higher inflation RAISE gross national happiness, which inverts the construct, and no source is given for this particular functional form. Gini is then explained (123-125). SSI (127-130) is (HS + GT)/TAX - health spending plus transfers over government revenue - asserted to lie in [0,1] with no check. GDP (134-138) is per-capita GDP as a living-standard proxy. CPI (139-146) is RLS x CSI: the religious living space index is 'a function of the number of nationalities n and the degree of freedom r' whose functional form is never given, and CSI = 0.28 HB + 0.39 WL + 0.32 OL is the cultural-value weights renormalised over three of the eight indicators, summing to 0.99. EPI (147-154) takes a Cobb-Douglas utility u(C,P) = C^a P^(1-a), takes logs, and calls the linear expression EPI = aC + (1-a)P with C climate similarity and P pollution - a log-utility used as an index, and 'pollution' entering positively, so dirtier air raises the environment pull unless P is signed negatively, which is never said. 155-160 build C from the APGAR newborn score (five indicators: summer temperature, summer precipitation, winter temperature, winter precipitation, seasonal difference) - an elegant borrowing that is never mapped to actual APGAR's 0-10 scale - and 161 is Figure 8's caption, 162 gives P = API. 163-164 then integrate: standardise, run AHP, and S = 0.1461 GNH + 0.2751 SSI + 0.4798 GDP + 0.0340 CPI + 0.0650 EPI (the weights sum to 1.0000 exactly, and Appendix A's matrix is said to give CR = 0.055). The weighting is the paper's central choice and it contradicts the paper's own thesis: culture pull, the reason the paper exists, receives 3.4% of the destination score, against 48.0% for GDP. Under those weights Maldives EDPs go where income is highest, which is exactly what the cultural-preservation argument was written to avoid. 165-167 add capacity and accessibility: a two-objective programme maximising destination suitability subject to an accessibility term written as 1 - Dij/Tij, where Dij is the death rate on the route and Tij the travel time - two quantities in different units subtracted from one, so the constraint is dimensionally undefined.

heading: 5 Models for Policies: Policies for UN and their Impacts (5.1 The Policies)
note: Four policy fields, one bullet each, before any model that justifies them. 168 is the chapter heading; 169 routes the section (EDPs are neither refugees nor immigrants, so the policies reflect national integrity and cultural uniqueness) and announces four fields and three sub-models. Economy (170-172): vocational training and equal jobs so EDPs enter the labour market - the policy that 5.2's effective-labour model then quantifies. Society (173-174): UN peacekeeping forces deployed to EDP areas to cut the crime rate and raise legal working time - an unusual and expensive instrument, and it is the only policy that 5.2's crime model touches, though the model contains no policing variable at all. Culture (175-178): lower or cancel language requirements of entry, and provide areas whose climate and geography resemble the original environment. Environment (179-181): economic and technical assistance to destination countries plus raised emissions standards 'within a reasonable range' - and note that raising a destination country's standards while Assumption 3 freezes per-capita emissions means the assistance, not the EDPs, has to pay for the tightening. The four bullets are the paper's actual deliverable to the UN, and the numbering of the models that follow (5.2 economy and society, 5.3 culture, 5.4 environment) maps one-to-one onto them, which is the paper's cleanest piece of structure.

heading: 5.2 The Impact of Economic and Social Policies (effective labor model, crime time-allocation model)
note: Two models, both imported, both estimated on Australia. 183 gives the mechanism the policies rest on: expansionary fiscal and monetary policy lets refugees enter production as labour, raising GDP and the domestic consumer market, while a high crime rate in 'a few European countries' causes unrest - a causal story with no citation and no data. Effective labour model: Y_t = A_t K_t^a H_t^b (184, cited to [8]), with H human capital, K capital and Y output (185); the contribution share is beta times the growth rate of H (186) and CHE = beta (dH/H) (Y/dY) (187); technological progress is unobservable, so a state-space AR(1) ln A_t = c + theta ln A_(t-1) + v_t is fitted (188-189, cited to [9]). Estimation on Australian GDP, capital stock and human capital stock 1990-2012 gives ln Y = ln A + 0.573 ln K + 0.923 ln H and ln A = -0.690 + 0.738 A_(t-1) (190-191), so beta = 0.923 (192); with H growth 2.41 and output growth 3.16, CHE = 2.41 x 0.923 / 3.16 = 70.4% (193-194, arithmetic correct). Then 195 draws the conclusion: for capital-intensive countries, absorbing immigrants is 'extremely beneficial' to GDP. Two checks the paper skips: alpha + beta = 0.573 + 0.923 = 1.496, i.e. strongly increasing returns, which contradicts 185's claim that alpha and beta are output shares (they must sum to 1); and a 70.4% human-capital contribution to growth over 1990-2012 is an implausibly high residual share that would normally be read as a specification problem rather than a finding. Crime model (196-218): crime is a rational time allocation (cited to Agnew 1992), income from legal and illegal work is concave, detection probability p, penalty f_i(t_i) concave (196-197); four states - employed and undetected, employed and detected, unemployed and undetected, unemployed and detected - give incomes I1-I4 with probabilities built from p and unemployment u (198-212); the individual maximises expected utility subject to t_i + t_l <= t0 (213-214); the Kuhn-Tucker conditions (215-216) and the implicit-function derivative dt*/dw < 0 (217) give the result in 218: more social welfare spending shortens time in illegal activity, so a small welfare payment cuts the refugee crime rate. Two gaps: the derivative holds w (the welfare payment) fixed in the state probabilities, so the sign comes from one term of a four-state expression that is printed corrupted, and the model has no policing term, so the peacekeeping-force policy of 5.1 is not what the model tests - it tests cash transfers instead.

heading: 5.3 The Impact of Cultural Policies (language attrition, cultural value score)
note: The cultural-impact chapter, and the weakest of the three: two policies, each measured by one formula or one number. 219 is the heading; 220 routes it (of the eight cultural indicators, many are policy-affected, per Figure 11) and opens Policy 1, lowering language requirements of entry, with UNESCO's definition of language extinction. 221 gives the attrition law NB = EDP_j (1 - DR)^t with NB in N (18) and 222 defines NB and DR; 223 then reverses the sign - if the community encourages its offspring, users grow - which 224 writes as NB = EDP_j (1 + BR)^t (19), with BR the birth rate, and 225 carries the tail of that equation plus Figure 9's caption ('The Policy-affected Indicators of Culture Value'). So the mechanical model of a language under policy is a single geometric series switched between a death rate and a birth rate: no threshold, no transmission between generations, and DR and BR are never estimated, so the 'extinction in decades' claim in 226 is not derived from the equation at all. 226 interprets (refusal to implement the language policy makes extinction likely, protection prevents 'huge loss of culture', shown in figure 12) and opens Policy 2, providing a similar living environment; 227 is Figure 10's caption (language users under two circumstances). 228 argues that similar environment preserves customs and cultural space and that only the composite CVS can capture the effect. 229 delivers the only computed number in the chapter: because custom activities, knowledge and practice and cultural space carry equal weight, each drop of one level in the range criterion or in the population criterion lowers the final CVS by 0.825 points - a linearisation of the scoring rule in 96 whose derivation is not shown (with eight equal-weight indicators the implied scale would be 12.5 points per indicator, not 0.825), and 229's tail glues the '5.4' heading.

heading: 5.4 The Impact of Environmental Policies (AR, PAP, CDE)
note: Four blocks, and the tightest model in the paper. 230 ties the policy to the Paris Agreement's NDCs and INDCs, defines the EDP accommodation rate AR = EDP_j / TP_j (20) and cites [12] for the NDC analysis, though no NDC data appear. 231 asks what is affected environmentally and, from the World Bank indicator list, takes PM2.5 air pollution and CO2 emissions. 232, explicitly invoking Assumption 3 (per-capita emissions unchanged), derives the post-arrival levels as population-weighted averages: PAP = (PAP_j TP_j + PAP_i EDP_i)/(TP_j + EDP_i) = PAP_j (1 - AR) + PAP_i AR (21), with the same expression for CDE - two lines of algebra that are correct, that need only the accommodation rate, and that show the model is a mixing rule rather than an environmental response model. 233 hands the result to the UN: raise destination countries' emission standards according to (21), and glues the '6 Application of the Models' heading. The chapter's honesty is notable relative to its neighbours - the mechanism is stated, the assumption it rests on is named, and the formula can be checked - but it also shows the limit of the whole policy part: the only quantified policy instrument is a dilution factor, and raising a country's standard while AR raises its average emissions is a rule that makes the standard rise as intake rises, i.e. the standard tracks the outcome instead of constraining it.

heading: 6 Application of the Models (6.1 Optimized Relocation Plans for Maldives)
note: The Maldives application, and the only place the paper produces a number it reports as a result. 234 sources the case: Maldives may be the first country submerged, and a 2012 interview with President Mohamed Nasheed gives three options - India, Australia, Sri Lanka (cited to [13]). 236 runs step 1 ('the results in table 13' - the table is numbered 1, so the cross-reference is wrong) and 237-238 hold Table 1's caption plus the watermark block with no text. 239 runs step 2, Z-score standardisation x' = (x - mu)/sigma (22), pointing to Appendix 2 for the calculation. 240-242 apply formula 7 and the allocation rule: assign to the highest S, and if the total exceeds 0.5% of the destination population, spill the remainder to the next country. 243 reports the outcome - S(Australia) > S(Sri Lanka) > S(India), 127,200 to Australia, 107,200 to Sri Lanka, 205,600 to India. Two checks against the paper's own rule. First, the 0.5% cap is violated for two of three destinations: 0.5% of Australia's 22.73 million is 113,650, below the 127,200 allocated, and 0.5% of Sri Lanka's 20.42 million is 102,100, below the 107,200 allocated - so the spill rule was not actually applied. Second, the three parts sum to 440,000, a total that appears nowhere in the paper: chapter 4.1 defines EDPs as the whole national population, the paper never states the Maldives population, and no figure in the extraction supports 440,000 (the country's 2014 population was about 400,000). The allocation therefore cannot be reproduced from the text, and the ranking that drives it rests on S with GDP weighted at 0.48.

heading: 6.2 Quantified Policies for UN
note: Six short blocks, the policy output. 244 is the heading. 245 puts each country's data into formulas 20 and 21 to get the intended new PAP and CDE 'in table 4'. 246 begins the conclusion sentence and is cut after seven words ('Therefore, when it comes to estimating EDP'), resuming in 249 across the two table captions (247, 248, both titled 'The Value of Standardized Indicators of India, Australia and Sri Lanka' - so Table 4's caption is a copy of Table 3's and the new PAP/CDE values are not described by it). 249 completes the sentence: to estimate destination countries' standards for greenhouse gas and pollutant emissions, the UN should raise the standards according to the data above - and glues the '7 Testing the model' heading. The chapter is honest about being a hand-off - the paper does not compute the new standards, it tells the UN to compute them - but the two tables that would carry the numbers are captioned identically and their contents are not in the extraction, so the quantified policy cannot be read off the paper at all.

heading: 7 Testing the model (7.1 consistency inspection of the pairwise matrix, 7.2 test of the effective labor model)
note: The only validation chapter, and it validates the two models that least need it. 251-256 run the AHP consistency test: CI = (lambda_max - n)/(n - 1) (23) with n = 5 (252), RI built by simulating 500 random 5x5 positive reciprocal matrices and averaging their largest eigenvalue (253), CR = CI/RI (25), and CR = 0.055 < 0.1 accepted (255-256). The arithmetic is checkable and slightly off: with lambda_max = 5.2203 (block 309), CI = 0.2203/4 = 0.0551, and the reported CR is 0.055, i.e. CR equals CI to three decimals, which implies RI = 1.00. The conventional random index for n = 5 is 1.12, which would give CR = 0.049 - still acceptable, so the conclusion survives, but the paper's simulated RI is never printed and the ratio is effectively reported as the index. The real problem is what is not tested: the consistency check says the five weights are internally coherent, not that GNH, SSI, GDP, CPI and EPI measure what they claim, and a consistent matrix of a misconceived index is still a misconceived index. 258-260 test the effective-labour model out of sample: elasticities fitted on 1990-2012, GDP re-predicted for 2013-2016, errors 4.3%, 2.4%, 1.4% and 3.1%, 'within acceptable limits' (260, whose tail glues '8 Strengths and Weaknesses / 8.1 Strengths'). Four out-of-sample years on one country is a thin validation, and the 70.4% contribution claim still has no confidence interval.

heading: 8 Strengths and Weaknesses (8.1 Strengths, 8.2 Weaknesses)
note: Four strengths and two weaknesses, each bullet split one printed line per block. Strengths: interdisciplinary sourcing - the 1951 Convention, the 1967 Protocol, the Paris Agreement, UNHCR's displaced-population classification, UNESCO's language-extinction definition, World Bank PM2.5 and CO2 (261-267); innovation by borrowing methods across fields - the IUCN Red List for culture value, the APGAR score for climate similarity (268-270, and these two borrowings are the paper's genuinely distinctive moves); cohesiveness, in that the eight cultural indicators feed both the relocation index and the cultural-policy model (271-274); and practical value, evidenced only by 'the results of Maldives simulation' (275-276, whose tail glues '8.2 Weaknesses'). Weaknesses, only two: no global-warming process is modelled, so sea level decades out is unknown (277-278); and no solution is offered for people moving because of climate impacts on agriculture (279-280, whose tail glues 'References'). The two admissions are real but far from the paper's actual exposure - the 0.5% allocation cap that is violated, the 440,000 total with no derivation, the GDP-dominated weights against the culture thesis, and the 0.5%-GDP contradiction are all unmentioned. References begin at block 281 and run to 307 (thirteen entries, several split across two blocks, one of which - [8] - has no journal). Appendix A follows at 308-309: the 5x5 pairwise matrix, the five weights (0.1461, 0.2751, 0.4798, 0.0340, 0.0650) and lambda_max = 5.2203, which is the audit trail behind block 164 and is the only place the matrix can be inspected. Appendix B at 310-315 gives the per-country indicator calculations and contains a clear unit error - 'India has a population of 126.6 billion' where 1.266 billion is meant, which is the figure later used in the 0.5% cap - plus an SSI calculation printed as 156.9 x 12.66 / 107,660,000,000,000 = 0.0199 whose numerator units do not match the definition in block 130.
